segments.text: A long-range ballistic missile spends most of its flight in space, falls back at several kilometers
a second, and from launch to impact can take less time than a lunch break. Somewhere in that half
hour, a defender has to notice a rocket launch on the far side of the planet, work out where it is
going, and fire another rocket that meets it in the vacuum above the atmosphere, close enough to
destroy it. The defender does not get a second look. Stopping a missile is not like catching a
ball, it is closer to catching a bullet with another bullet from a continent away. So here is
the question, how does anyone defend against something this fast, and why does the defense
always seem to cost more than the attack? The answer comes as a chain of stages, because a missile's
flight has distinct parts, and each part allows one kind of defense and rules out another. Each stage
exists because the one before it cannot be trusted to do the whole job. Start with the first stage,
which is knowing. A long-range missile in its boost phase burns a huge rocket motor for a few minutes,
and that flame is bright in infrared. Satellites in high orbit watch the Earth for exactly that heat,
and when one sees it, the alarm goes out within moments. These satellites cannot say where the missile
will land. They can say that it has started, and roughly where from, and that is a great deal. Every
minute gained here is a minute of the 30 that the defender has to work with. Next comes the question of
what the missile is going to do. Large radars, the ones with a flat face the size of a building,
pick up the missile as it climbs above the horizon and follow it along its path. A ballistic missile
is predictable. Once the engine stops, it follows an arc governed by gravity, and a good radar can
calculate where it will land from a few seconds of track. This is both the strength and the weakness
of the missile. Its path is nearly perfect, so it can be hit, and nearly perfectly known,
so it can be hit by something fired in advance. The boost phase would be the best time to strike,
if it could be reached. The missile is large, slow and bright, it has not yet released any decoys,
and a single hit would destroy everything it carries. The catch is geography. To be there in those few
minutes, a defender needs a launcher or an aircraft within a few hundred cometers of the launch site,
which is usually inside the territory of the one who launched it. So the best window is the one that is
hardest to use, and defenses are designed for the later ones. The third stage is the interceptor.
In space, an interceptor does not explode near its target the way an air defense missile does.
Closing speeds of many kilometers a second leave no room for that, and the explosion would not do
the job in a vacuum anyway. So it hits the warhead directly. A small vehicle separates from the rocket,
carries its own sensor and tiny thrusters, steers itself onto the target and destroys it with the
force of the collision. This is called hit-to-kill, and it is why it has been compared to a bullet
meeting a bullet. That gives rise to the next question, which is how to tell a warhead from
everything around it. A missile in space does not arrive alone. The upper stage of the rocket tumbles
along beside it, and the attacker may release decoys, light balloons that move the same way as the real
warhead in a vacuum, or small pieces of metal that fill the sky with echoes. In the near vacuum,
a feather and a hammer fall the same way, so the usual difference between a heavy thing and a light
thing disappears. The interceptor has to decide which of ten objects is the real one in a matter
of seconds, and it cannot afford to be wrong. This difficulty is why the defense has more than one
chance. If the object is not destroyed in space, it comes down into the atmosphere, where the air
strips away light decoys, and the warhead is left alone, falling at high speed. At that point,
a different kind of interceptor takes over, one that engages in the last few tens of commonly.
The last stage is the most reliable, because there is little time for countermeasures,
but it is also the one with the least time, and it protects only a small area, and a miss means
impact. The geometry of this arrangement has an important consequence. Each type of interceptor
can only defend a certain footprint, which means the whole country cannot be covered by one kind,
and the choices of where to put the batteries are choices about what to protect. Defending a city and
defending a base are different problems. Even a very good system has an edge, and the attacker is
able to choose where to aim. Where the launchers stand matters as well. A ship carrying interceptors
and a powerful radar can sail to the position that covers a threat and move again when the threat moves.
A fixed site in a country cannot. This is why naval missile defense is often used to cover allies far
from home, and why the destroyer that is doing it cannot be doing other jobs at the same time.
A hull committed to watching the sky above a coast is a hull that is not escorting a carrier.
That brings in the question of numbers. Interceptors are expensive, and each is fired
in pairs or more, because the cost of a miss is much higher than the cost of a second missile.
An attacker who sends a few dozen cheap missiles and decoys can drain a magazine that took years to build.
This is the reason a lot of effort goes into making defense cheaper, shooting only at those missiles
that threaten something of value, and ignoring those aimed at empty ground. A defender who spends
a premium to answer every launch will run out of money before the attacker runs out of rockets.
Not every missile follows this path, and the difference is worth stating. A cruise missile is more like a
small jet, it flies low and slow for hours, hugging the ground, and a ballistic defense is of no
use against it. It falls to the air defense layers from the earlier video in this series.
A real attack often combines both, so that a defender must choose between watching the heights
and watching the ground. There is a short range version of the same idea that most people have
seen on television. Rockets fired over a border at a city fly for under a minute, so an air defense
radar tracks each one, a computer works out where it will land, and only those headed for an inhabited
area are engaged. The rest are allowed to fall in fields. It is a defense built around saying no,
and the decision of which rockets are not worth a missile is part of the weapon.
The newest weapon complicates the picture. Hypersonic glide vehicles are launched on a rocket,
then separate and glide through the upper atmosphere at very high speed, maneuvering as they go.
They do not follow the predictable arc. Defenders cannot easily say where they will land until late,
and they fly at altitudes that are too low for space interceptors and too high for many missiles designed
to stop aircraft. The same radars that were built to compute a smooth curve are forced to follow
something that deliberately will not draw one. Testing is the part nobody can see clearly. In a trial,
the target is launched at a known time from a known place, and the defender knows roughly what to
expect. In war, none of that holds. Public test records of the large systems have been mixed,
with successes and failures, and the failures are as useful to the engineers as the successes.
A defense that has hit its target in the exercises has shown it can work, and not that it will on the
day, against a missile that was launched to defeat it. Which brings us to what is easy to get wrong.
A missile defense system is often discussed as a shield, either perfect or useless. It is neither.
It is a sensor network and a set of limited magazines, which tilts the odds in the defender's
favor for a given number of attackers. That is my own reading, but it suggests that the main effect
of such a system is on the mind of the person deciding to attack. They no longer know whether
the missile will arrive, and a plan that depends on every missile arriving is a plan that has become
uncertain. So return to the 30 minutes between the launch and the impact. Every part, the satellite
that sees the flame, the radar that draws the arc, the interceptor that hits in space, the one that
waits for the last few kilometers and the decision that most of the sky can be ignored, is there to
buy time to look again. Missile defense is not a wall. It is a series of second chances,
chances. And the attacker does not know how many remain.
